prompt: Ana's request to S3 is signed correctly, and S3 refuses it with the code AccessDenied. Which gate refused it?
hint: One gate asks who; the other asks whether.

choices.text: Authentication: AccessDenied means her key was not recognised
choices.why: A key S3 cannot verify stops at the first gate with a code of its own, such as SignatureDoesNotMatch.

choices.text: Authentication, because her session was opened without MFA
choices.why: Whether MFA was used is a circumstance, and circumstances are tested by policy conditions at the second gate. Her identity was known.

choices.text: Authorisation: S3 knew who she was, and nothing allowed the request
choices.why: Right. The signature passed the first gate; AccessDenied is the answer of the second, after reading every policy that applies.

choices.text: Neither: a security group dropped it on the way to S3
choices.why: A security group filters packets to your own machines. S3 answered with a code, so the request reached its API.

prompt: Match each part of a request to its value in the lesson's example.
hint: Who, what, which thing, under what circumstances.

pairs.right: the session was opened with MFA

prompt: A virtual machine sits behind a security group that allows no inbound traffic at all. A leaked access key allows ec2:TerminateInstances on it. Can the key's holder delete the machine?
hint: Where does that request go?

choices.text: Yes: the call goes to the provider's API, which the security group never sees
choices.why: Right. A security group judges packets to the machine; deleting it is an API call to the provider, judged by policies.

choices.text: No: with no inbound traffic allowed, nothing can reach it
choices.why: That is true of packets to the machine. The delete request is never sent to the machine at all.

choices.text: Only from inside the machine's own network
choices.why: The provider's API is reached over the internet, from anywhere the key is.

choices.text: Only if the key also allows ssh to the machine
choices.why: ssh is a way into the operating system. Terminating is done to the machine from outside, by the provider.

prompt: Which statement about the AWS root user is true?
hint: Policies are the brakes.

choices.text: It obeys the same group policies as any administrator
choices.why: Root belongs to no group and is not limited by the account's policies.

choices.text: It is created by the first administrator the owner sets up
choices.why: It is the other way round: root exists first, from the sign-up, and creates everything else.

choices.text: It stops working once another administrator exists
choices.why: Root keeps working for good; that is why it has to be locked away rather than forgotten.

choices.text: No permission policy inside its own account limits it
choices.why: Right. Policies are how an account limits its identities, and the root user is the one they do not apply to.

prompt: Rita runs a one-person company and signs in as root every day, with MFA. What is the strongest reason for her to stop?
hint: Think about the worst session, not the usual one.

choices.text: Root cannot use the command line at all, so every script she writes needs another identity
choices.why: Root can have access keys; the advice is that it should not.

choices.text: A mistake or a stolen session as root has no limit, and root is also her way back in
choices.why: Right. Every root session can do anything, and it is the identity that recovers the account; losing it loses both.

choices.text: The provider charges more for calls made as root
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson ties root to the bill. The argument is about damage and recovery.

choices.text: MFA on root can expire and lock her out of the account
choices.why: A second factor does not expire on its own. What locks people out is losing it, which is why root's is kept safe.

prompt: Eight people each have the same three policies attached to their own users. The team stops needing one of the three. How many detachments does removing it take?
hint: One per person who carries it.

prompt: On Paulo's last day his console sign-in is disabled. On Monday a script on his laptop still uploads files to the account. Why?
hint: How many credentials can a user have?

choices.text: Console sessions keep working for a week after a password is disabled
choices.why: The script is not using a console session at all; it signs with an access key.

choices.text: The script runs as his group, which he still belongs to
choices.why: A group has no credentials and cannot make a call; only identities can.

choices.text: His access key is separate, and disabling the password left it active
choices.why: Right. Password and access keys are independent; the complete change deactivates the keys or deletes the user.

choices.text: Disabling a user only takes effect at the next access review of the account
choices.why: Changes to credentials take effect when made. The review is how people find what was missed.

prompt: A permission has to say that the analysts may read one bucket. Where does it go at AWS?
hint: What can a group be, and what can it not be?

choices.text: In a policy attached to the analysts' group
choices.why: Right. A group is how permissions are handed to a set of people; a new analyst gets it by joining.

choices.text: In a bucket policy that names the group as the Principal
choices.why: A policy cannot name a group as its principal at AWS. The group is reached by attaching the policy to it.

choices.text: On every analyst's own user, since a group cannot hold policies
choices.why: Holding policies is exactly what a group is for; attaching one per person is the habit that goes wrong.

choices.text: In a smaller group nested inside the analysts' group
choices.why: IAM groups cannot contain other groups.

prompt: What does a caller receive when it assumes a role?
hint: Nobody logs in to a role.

choices.text: The role's password, to sign in to the console with
choices.why: A role has no password; that is what makes it different from a user.

choices.text: Temporary credentials that act as the role until they expire
choices.why: Right. A key id, a secret, a session token and an expiry, from STS.

choices.text: A permanent copy of the role's permissions on the caller's own user
choices.why: Nothing is copied onto the caller. It acts as the role, for a while, and then stops.

choices.text: A long-lived access key whose id begins with AKIA
choices.why: AKIA is the prefix of a user's long-lived key. A role's temporary credentials begin with ASIA.

prompt: By default, how many minutes does a session from sts:AssumeRole last?
hint: The figure's step 3 says it in hours.

prompt: The policy on a role that says which principals may assume it is its ___ policy.
hint: The other one says what the role may do.

prompt: A virtual machine uses a role to read a bucket. Put the steps in order.
hint: The figure in this section, top to bottom.
items: The machine signs an sts:AssumeRole request as itself
STS checks the role's trust policy
STS returns a key id, a secret, a session token and an expiry
The machine signs its S3 call with those credentials
S3 checks the call against the role's permission policy
trap: The permission policy is not read when the role is assumed. It is read by S3, on every call made with the credentials.

prompt: A role's permission policy allows s3:* on every bucket, and its trust policy names only ec2.amazonaws.com. A developer wants to assume it from her laptop. What happens?
hint: Both documents have to say yes.

choices.text: She can, because the permission policy allows everything in S3
choices.why: The permission policy decides what the role does once assumed. Who may assume it is the other document's question.

choices.text: She can, but her session is capped at fifteen minutes
choices.why: Fifteen minutes is the shortest session anyone may ask for, not a penalty. She gets none.

choices.text: She can if she signed in with MFA first
choices.why: A second factor proves who she is. It does not add her to a trust policy that names only a service.

choices.text: She cannot: the trust policy does not name her
choices.why: Right. However much the role may do, only the principals its trust policy names can become it.

prompt: In a policy statement, the key whose value is Allow or Deny is called ___.
hint: It is the second line of each statement in the example.

prompt: One statement lists three actions and two resources. How many action-and-resource pairs does it cover?
hint: The lists multiply.

prompt: Match each element of a policy to what it holds.
hint: Six elements; four of them here.

pairs.right: the version of the policy language
the things covered, written as ARNs
the circumstances in which it applies

right_distractors: the date the policy was last edited

prompt: A statement allows s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::example-reports/* and the user's listing is refused. Why?
hint: What kind of resource does a listing act on?

choices.text: ListBucket acts on the bucket, and that ARN names only objects inside it
choices.why: Right. The resource for a listing is the bucket's own ARN, with no /* after it.

choices.text: Every listing needs an s3:prefix condition to work, and this statement has none
choices.why: The condition narrows what may be listed. Without one the listing covers the whole bucket, and is allowed.

choices.text: The Version line is missing, so the statement is ignored
choices.why: Without Version the policy is read in the older language, not ignored, and the question never said it was missing.

choices.text: Listing also needs s3:GetObject on the same ARN
choices.why: Reading objects and listing them are separate actions; neither needs the other.

prompt: A policy attached to the role report-reader has no Principal element. What does that mean?
hint: Which kinds of policy need to name somebody?

choices.text: It applies to every principal in the account
choices.why: A policy with no Principal is not a policy for everybody; it is attached to one identity and speaks for it.

choices.text: It is invalid until a Principal element is added
choices.why: Adding one would be the mistake: identity policies do not carry that element.

choices.text: Nothing: the role itself is the principal
choices.why: Right. An identity policy is about the identity it is attached to. Trust and resource policies are the ones that name principals.

choices.text: It applies only to the root user of the account
choices.why: Root is not limited by policies at all, so no policy is written for it.

prompt: Ana's group allows s3:DeleteObject on a bucket. A policy on Ana's own user denies s3:DeleteObject there. She tries to delete an object. What happens?
hint: Rule 3.

choices.text: Allowed: the group's policy was attached first
choices.why: Order of attachment, like order of writing, changes nothing.

choices.text: Refused: a matching explicit Deny wins over every Allow
choices.why: Right. Where each policy is attached makes no difference; the Deny ends the question.

choices.text: Allowed: when two policies disagree, the more generous one applies
choices.why: It is the reverse. A disagreement between an Allow and a Deny always ends in the Deny.

choices.text: Allowed: a group policy outranks a policy on one user
choices.why: There is no ranking between where policies sit; their statements are pooled.

prompt: No policy that applies to Ana mentions s3:PutObject. She tries to upload a file. What happens?
hint: Where does every request start?

choices.text: Allowed, because nothing forbids it
choices.why: The default runs the other way: a request needs something to allow it.

choices.text: Refused, and an explicit Deny is added to her policy
choices.why: Nothing is written into her policy. An implicit deny is the absence of an Allow, not a statement.

choices.text: Allowed if her group can read the same bucket
choices.why: Reading and uploading are separate actions; an Allow for one says nothing about the other.

choices.text: Refused, by the implicit deny
choices.why: Right. Nothing allowed it, so it stays where every request starts.

prompt: Put the steps of deciding a request in order.
hint: The figure in this section, from the top.
items: A matching explicit Deny, if any, refuses it
Otherwise, a matching Allow grants it
Otherwise, it stays denied by default
trap: Looking for an Allow before the Deny gets the answer wrong whenever both match: the Deny has to be able to win.

prompt: Ana's group allows s3:* on the bucket example-reports. Her own policy denies s3:DeleteObject there. Which of her requests succeed? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Deny removes only what it names; the Allow covers only what it names.

choices.text: s3:GetObject on an object in example-reports
choices.why: Allowed: s3:* covers it and the Deny does not name it.

choices.text: s3:DeleteObject on an object in example-reports
choices.why: Refused: the explicit Deny matches, and nothing undoes it.

choices.text: s3:PutObject on an object in example-reports
choices.why: Allowed: s3:* includes uploading, and only deletion was denied.

choices.text: s3:GetObject on an object in another bucket
choices.why: Refused, implicitly: the group's Allow names only example-reports.

prompt: A statement denies s3:DeleteObject with the condition Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent false. A script signing with a long-lived access key deletes an object, and it works. Why?
hint: What does a request signed with a long-lived key carry about MFA?

choices.text: Deny statements apply to console sessions and never to access keys
choices.why: A Deny applies to every request it matches, however it was signed. This one did not match.

choices.text: The script's own Allow was more specific than the Deny
choices.why: Specificity decides nothing. A matching Deny would have won over any Allow.

choices.text: The request carried no MFA key at all, so Bool had nothing to compare and the Deny did not apply
choices.why: Right. That is why the section writes BoolIfExists: a missing key then counts as a match.

choices.text: A signed request always counts as MFA present
choices.why: A signature proves the key, not a second factor; the key is simply absent from such requests.

prompt: A backup job's policy includes iam:* on *. The job never touches IAM. Why is that line the worst one in the policy?
hint: What can an identity do if it can change identities?

choices.text: It lets the job read every bucket's contents without any S3 permission
choices.why: IAM actions change identities and policies; reading objects is an S3 action. The danger is that it can grant itself that too.

choices.text: IAM calls are billed per request, and a wildcard can run up the bill
choices.why: The problem is what the line allows, not what it costs.

choices.text: It stops any other policy from being attached to the job's role
choices.why: Nothing in IAM works that way; it would rather let the job attach anything it likes.

choices.text: It can give itself any permission, so it amounts to administrator access
choices.why: Right. Attaching an administrator policy to its own role, or creating a user with keys, is one call away.

prompt: Why is "Action": "s3:Get*" riskier than it looks?
hint: Read the name as a pattern, and think about next year.

choices.text: It matches every S3 action, because a star ends the name
choices.why: The pattern keeps its prefix: only actions whose names begin with Get match.

choices.text: It matches every Get action, even ones added later
choices.why: Right. GetBucketPolicy is in it today, and whatever S3 adds tomorrow will be too.

choices.text: It is invalid, since wildcards are allowed only in resources
choices.why: Wildcards are allowed in actions, which is exactly why this line needs reading.

choices.text: It matches only s3:GetObject, so listing breaks
choices.why: It matches far more than GetObject; listing is ListBucket, which it does not cover.

prompt: Reviewing the policy of a job that only uploads files to one bucket, which lines should stop you? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section's list of lines to stop at.

choices.text: "Resource": "*"
choices.why: Every resource in the account, where the job needs one bucket.

choices.text: "Action": "s3:PutObject"
choices.why: That is the one action the job needs.

choices.text: "Action": "iam:CreateUser"
choices.why: An uploading job has no reason to create identities, and a new user with keys is a way in.

choices.text: "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::example-backups/nightly/*"
choices.why: One prefix of one bucket: the narrow resource the job should have.

choices.text: "Action": "s3:*"
choices.why: Every S3 operation, deleting buckets and rewriting their policies included, for a job that uploads.

prompt: A broad grant added to the on-call role during an incident eighteen months ago is still there. Nobody has complained about it. What should the review do?
hint: What does unused access produce, until the day it is used?

choices.text: Remove it: unused access only surfaces when abused
choices.why: Right. If it turns out to be needed, the refusal names the action and it comes back as one line.

choices.text: Keep it: eighteen months without a complaint shows it is harmless
choices.why: A policy that allows too much never produces a complaint. Silence is the symptom, not the proof.

choices.text: Keep it until the provider marks it as expired
choices.why: Grants do not expire unless somebody makes them; only role sessions do.

choices.text: Add a Deny beside it, so the grant can be restored quickly
choices.why: Two statements that cancel out are harder to read than none. Removing it is the change.

prompt: In the lesson's capture, how many sources did the CLI search for credentials before it gave up?
hint: Count the lines of the --debug output.

prompt: Put these credential sources in the order the AWS CLI searched them in the capture.
hint: The environment first; the machine's own last.
trap: The metadata service is last, which is why a forgotten key in the environment wins over a machine's role.

prompt: A virtual machine has a narrowly scoped role. Months ago somebody set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in its environment for a test. Which credentials does the CLI on it sign with?
hint: Which end of the chain is the environment on?

choices.text: The role, because a machine's own credentials always take priority
choices.why: The machine's sources are the last two of twelve. Everything above them wins.

choices.text: Both, with their permissions combined
choices.why: One request is signed with one set of credentials; nothing merges two identities.

choices.text: The key in the environment, which the chain reads before the metadata service
choices.why: Right. The first source that answers is used, and the environment comes first; the role is never asked.

choices.text: Neither: two sources conflict, so the CLI refuses
choices.why: The chain does not look for conflicts. It stops at the first source that answers.

prompt: In the capture, what did aws sts get-caller-identity do with no credentials available?
hint: Read the error's name.

choices.text: It asked AWS over the network, which answered that the caller was unknown
choices.why: An unknown caller would be the first gate refusing at AWS. This refusal never left the laptop.

choices.text: It refused on the laptop before signing, so nothing was sent to AWS
choices.why: Right. NoCredentials is the CLI's own refusal: with nothing to sign with, there was no request to send.

choices.text: It sent the request unsigned, as an anonymous caller
choices.why: The CLI does not send an unsigned call here; it stops and says why.

choices.text: It used the example key from the documentation
choices.why: That key appears only in the last block, written into a file on purpose, and no call was made with it.

prompt: An access key id begins with ASIA. What kind of credential is it?
hint: Compare it with the id in the credentials file.

choices.text: A long-lived key that belongs to a user
choices.why: That is AKIA, the prefix of the key in the lesson's credentials file.

choices.text: A key that only works in the Asia Pacific regions
choices.why: The prefix says what kind of credential it is, not where it may be used.

choices.text: A key that belongs to the root user of the account
choices.why: Root should have no key at all, and the prefix does not name an identity.

choices.text: A temporary one, such as a role hands out
choices.why: Right. ASIA marks temporary credentials; a user's long-lived key begins with AKIA.

prompt: Put the steps of a federated sign-in in order.
hint: The numbered list in this section.
items: Ana signs in at the organisation's identity provider, with a second factor
The identity provider sends a signed statement of who she is and her groups
The cloud provider checks the signature and maps her groups to roles
Ana receives temporary credentials for one of those roles
trap: The cloud provider never sees her password: the only thing it checks is the identity provider's signature.

prompt: Ana is disabled at the identity provider at 10:00. At 09:30 she had assumed a role for a one-hour session. What can she still do?
hint: The section names one honest gap.

choices.text: Nothing: disabling her revokes every credential at once
choices.why: Disabling stops new sign-ins. A session already issued is not recalled by it.

choices.text: Sign in again, since the cloud keeps its own copy of her password
choices.why: With federation the cloud keeps no password for her; the identity provider is the only door.

choices.text: Use those role credentials until they expire at 10:30
choices.why: Right. Credentials already handed out work until they expire, which is the argument for short sessions.

choices.text: Keep using the credentials for a year, like an access key
choices.why: Role credentials carry an expiry; hers ran out at 10:30.

prompt: Ana types her password into a convincing fake sign-in page. Which second factor would still keep the attacker out?
hint: Which factor checks the site it is talking to?

choices.text: A hardware security key, which answers only to the site it was registered with
choices.why: Right. The fake page is a different site, so the key gives it nothing to replay.

choices.text: An authenticator app, since its code changes every thirty seconds
choices.why: The fake page can ask for today's code too and use it at once, within those thirty seconds.

choices.text: A code sent to her phone by text message
choices.why: It can be typed into the fake page like any other code, and the number itself can be moved.

choices.text: A longer password, changed every month
choices.why: A password of any length is typed into the fake page just the same, and it is not a second factor.

prompt: A build pipeline deploys to an account with an access key stored in its settings. What change removes the key altogether?
hint: The third line of the credential chain.

choices.text: Encrypting the key in the pipeline's settings
choices.why: An encrypted key is still a key the pipeline can read and anyone who takes over the pipeline can use.

choices.text: A role, assumed with a token issued per run
choices.why: Right. The account trusts the platform in a role's trust policy, and there is no stored key left to leak.

choices.text: Rotating the key every ninety days, on a schedule
choices.why: Rotation shortens how long a leaked key works. The key is still there.

choices.text: Moving the key into an environment variable instead
choices.why: The environment is the first place the chain looks, and the key is just as stored there.

prompt: Match each Google Cloud or Azure idea to its name there.
hint: The table in this section.

pairs.left: Google Cloud's identity for a program
Azure's grant of a role at a scope

prompt: At Google Cloud, a program such as a virtual machine runs as a ___ account.
hint: The table's last row.

prompt: At Azure, the identity created for a virtual machine or a function, with credentials the platform rotates, is a ___ identity.
hint: The table's last row.

prompt: At Google Cloud, Bruno is granted the basic role Editor on a folder that holds twelve projects. What can he change?
hint: Which way do bindings travel?

choices.text: Only the folder's own settings, not the projects inside it
choices.why: That would be true if bindings did not travel down. They do.

choices.text: Nothing at all until he first assumes the Editor role, the way it works at AWS
choices.why: At Google Cloud a role is something he is given, not an identity he becomes.

choices.text: Only projects created in the folder after the grant
choices.why: Inheritance covers what is below the folder now as well as what is added later.

choices.text: Nearly everything in all twelve projects, because the binding is inherited
choices.why: Right. A binding applies to everything below where it was made, and Editor is broad.

prompt: At AWS, the service that records the calls made to the API is ___.
hint: Its Google Cloud counterpart is Cloud Audit Logs.

prompt: Why send the audit log to storage in a separate account?
hint: Who could otherwise remove it?

choices.text: Because the provider refuses to keep logs in the audited account
choices.why: It keeps them there by default. Moving them is a decision about who can delete them.

choices.text: So the administrators it audits cannot erase their own tracks
choices.why: Right. A log its subjects can erase records only what they chose to leave.

choices.text: So that reads of data get recorded, which they are not by default
choices.why: Recording reads is a separate setting; where the log is stored does not turn it on.

choices.text: Because entries kept in the same account expire after a day
choices.why: The defaults keep ninety days of changes at AWS and Azure. The reason is who can delete them.

prompt: Objects in a bucket were read by somebody who should not have read them. The account has CloudTrail on its default settings. What will its log show about the reads?
hint: Which kind of call is recorded without anybody asking?

choices.text: Every GetObject call of the last ninety days
choices.why: Ninety days is the default for calls that change things. Reads of objects are not among them.

choices.text: The reads, but without saying who made them
choices.why: When a call is recorded, the principal is the first thing in the entry. These were not recorded at all.

choices.text: No record of them, since reads of data were never configured to be logged
choices.why: Right. GetObject is a data event, and AWS records those only when somebody sets it up.

choices.text: Only the reads that were refused with AccessDenied
choices.why: Refusals are recorded for the calls that are logged. Reads of data are not logged by default, allowed or refused.

prompt: A function has to read the objects under one prefix of one bucket. Which design follows this lesson?
hint: What kind of identity, and how much should it allow?

choices.text: An access key in an environment variable, scoped to that prefix
choices.why: The scope is right and the credential is not: a stored long-lived key is what a role exists to replace.

choices.text: An execution role whose policy allows s3:GetObject on that prefix
choices.why: Right. A role gives temporary credentials with no key to store, and the policy allows the one action on the one prefix.

choices.text: The credentials of the developer who wrote it, since she already has access
choices.why: The function would act as her, with everything she may do, and the log would blame her for its calls.

choices.text: An execution role with s3:* on every resource, to be narrowed later
choices.why: Later rarely comes; start from nothing and add the one action.

prompt: A program on a virtual machine reads a bucket through the machine's role. Which two documents both have to say yes?
hint: One lets it in, the other lets it act.

choices.text: The machine's security group and the bucket's policy
choices.why: A security group filters packets to the machine; it has no say over calls to the storage API.

choices.text: The root user's approval and the group's policy
choices.why: Root approves nothing day to day, and a machine belongs to no group.

choices.text: The trust policy and the owner's console password
choices.why: A role has no password, and nobody's password is involved when a machine assumes one.

choices.text: Its trust policy and its permission policy
choices.why: Right. The trust policy lets the machine assume the role; the permission policy lets the role read.

prompt: Inside one account, Bruno's user has no policies attached. The bucket policy of example-reports allows his user s3:GetObject. Can he read an object there?
hint: Where can an Allow come from inside one account?

choices.text: Yes, the Allow on the resource suffices
choices.why: Right. Across accounts both sides would have to allow it; in one account either side can.

choices.text: No: a user with no policies is refused everything
choices.why: His own policies are not the only place an Allow can come from; the bucket's policy counts too.

choices.text: No: a bucket policy can deny but never allow
choices.why: Resource policies can do both; this one names his user and allows the action.

choices.text: Only after he assumes a role that the bucket trusts
choices.why: Nothing here involves a role; the bucket policy names his user directly.
